Prevention: Prevention
Test for wireworms in soil at least one week before planting by using germinating seed bait (GBS):
Mix corn and wheat seed - 50:50.
Soak mixture in water for 24 hours.
Place mixture in a hole in the soil, about 10 cm deep, 25 cm wide
Spread half a cup of the mixture across the bottom of the whole.
Wireworms will be attracted to the germinating seed
Fill the hole in with soil, leaving a soil mound
Cover the mound with a 50 cm square piece of black plastic.
Secure by covering the edges with soil
Cover the black plastic with a 1 m square sheet of clear plastic and secure by covering edges with soil.
This will keep the soil below warm and speed up germination.
Place a flag or marker next to the mound so it can be located
Place four
GBS traps per hectare, or a minimum of 10 in a field.
Examine traps after one week in the soil.
If more than one wireworm per trap is found there is a high probability that damage will occur to corn seeds and seedlings.
In this instance, plant a less susceptible crop such as a winter cereal instead, or plant maize in an uninfested field if possible.
Do not grow maize in an infested area for at least two years
Plant maize when weather conditions are optimal (do not plant early).
Otherwise germination may be slow making seedlings more susceptible to wireworm infestation
Use press wheels at sowing, set at 2-4 kg cm-1 width after planting rain or 4-8 kg per cm in dry soil.
Wireworms prefer cultivated soil.
To prevent the spread of the pest, avoid rotating or planting near alternative hosts.
Wireworm attacks most field crops, including oilseeds, grain legumes and cereals.
Also canola, potatoes, tomatoes, carrots, coffee, rice, grapes, sunflowers
Monitoring: Click beetles, black or dark brown, about 3 mm wide, 10 mm long - dimensions vary with species
Cylindrical, hardened, shiny generally cream to yellow brown in colour, about 1-2 mm wide, 10-20 mm long - dimensions vary with species
Hollowed out seeds (due to larvae feeding on them)
Plants turning purple, wilting and breaking at the soil surface (larvae bore into the stalk)
Ring-barking or complete cutting of stem due to feeding adults.
Adults chew on seedlings at or above ground level
Gaps in stands due to larvae attacking germinating seeds and seedling roots and shoots
